transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-21 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Sofia Patel (Redwood SE), Martin Lopez (BrightLayer Eng Mgr), Priya Shah (BLH ML Eng), Olivia Chen (BLH DevOps)

Summary:
Quick hosted API demo focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming behavior, key parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), and practical retry/backoff patterns. Customer wanted assurances on latency, data residency and an ops-friendly console walkthrough for Optimize recommendations.

Topics covered:
- Hosted API streaming semantics and how to consume partial tokens
- Parameter trade-offs for quality vs cost and latency
- Retry/backoff patterns and idempotency suggestions
- Console tour: traces, token cost breakdown, per-route dashboards
- Proposed POC scope and compliance questions (SOC2, data residency)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna run through a live hosted API demo, chat and text generation basics, stream handling, and some retry patterns — and we'll hit the console at the end. Sofia and I will tag-team.
[00:18] Martin: Awesome, thanks. Quick thing up front, our timeline is tight, three month POC ideally, and we need to keep PII on-prem or in the EU-east region.
[00:27] Jordan: Got it, makes sense. We'll note EU residency, and we do have private deployment options, but for a POC hosted can run in eu-central region.
[00:34] Priya: Hi, I'm mainly interested in throughput for our chat use-case, we expect bursts of like 500-1k concurrent sessions.
[00:44] Sofia: Great, for bursts we usually recommend a mix of reserved capacity and burst config. For the hosted API you can combine route-based rate limits and batching on our side; we'll show the console Optimize hints.
[00:59] Jordan: Ok let's jump to a quick code sample. (shares screen) This is a minimal streaming client. Note how we open the websocket / SSE stream and parse partial responses — you should be prepared to handle mid-token updates and re-assemble.
[01:20] Jordan: (typing) Example: request body fields: model, messages, max_tokens, temperature, top_p, and stream: true. Also highlight idempotency-key header if you want safe retries.
[01:38] Martin: When there's an interruption mid-stream, do we re-request with the same idempotency key or do we append context?
[01:45] Sofia: We usually recommend resuming from the last confirmed token client-side, then either request a continuation or — simpler — re-issue the request with the same prompt plus the last accepted output as context. The idempotency key prevents duplicate billing for completed tokens.
[02:06] Olivia: Docs mention KV cache — is that like a prefix cache on your side?
[02:10] Jordan: Yes, KV cache is used for key-value cache of past tokens for faster context reuse, but the transcript system sometimes writes that as K V cash, ha. On hosted we do automatic prefix caching for repeated contexts which reduces token compute for warm sessions.
[02:30] Priya: Any guidance on temperature/top_p defaults for customer support chat vs creative generation?
[02:36] Sofia: For ticket triage you'd keep temperature around 0.0-0.2 and lower top_p to keep the model deterministic. For creative responses bump temp to 0.8 and top_p 0.9. Increasing max_tokens increases latency/cost linearly, so be deliberate.
[02:58] Jordan: Also covered in Optimize: the console suggests quantization or model variant changes if your workload is throughput-bound. We'll show that report.
[03:10] Martin: About retries — what's Redwood's recommended backoff curve?
[03:14] Sofia: We recommend exponential backoff with jitter: e.g., initial 200ms, then 500ms, 1.2s, 3s, capped around 10s, and failover to a cheaper model variant if persistent. For streaming, don't re-stream from scratch too aggressively; prefer resume + short continuation.
[03:38] Priya: Are there idempotency caveats with streaming?
[03:42] Jordan: Right — streaming is inherently partial; idempotency covers completed responses. For interrupted streams you should preserve the partial result client-side and then request a continuation; our SDKs help with that pattern.
[03:58] Martin: Can you demo a failure mode? Like a mid-generation error and how client should behave?
[04:02] Sofia: Sure — I'll force a 500 and show how the SDK surfaces that. (demo) You see the partial tokens, then error. The recommended client flow: show partial to user if acceptable, record telemetry, then either retry with backoff or call fallback route (cheaper model) depending on business logic.
[05:10] Jordan: Quick console jump — here's the per-route dashboard. You can filter by model and see token-level cost and latency percentiles. For POC we'll give you access to a demo project so you can see these charts for your calls.
[05:40] Olivia: How granular is the audit trail? We need per-request audit logs for compliance.
[05:45] Jordan: We provide request-level logs with redaction controls. For SOC2 customers we keep full audit trails and can integrate with your SIEM via secure log shipping.
[05:58] Martin: Does Redwood have a SOC 2 cert?
[06:01] Sofia: Yes we do, and we'll share the attestation — the security FAQ link is in the follow-ups. Sometimes the transcript service reads that as sock two, so don't worry about the weird auto-cap.
[06:15] Priya: For the POC we'll probably run a small dataset through to check quality regressions. Can Optimize suggest quantization profiles without affecting output quality too much?
[06:25] Jordan: Optimize can run a quick recommendation based on work-load signatures — sequence lengths, token distributions. It suggests quantization levels and whether a different model family will be cost-efficient. It's conservative: it flags potential quality regressions and ties them back to your prompt evals.
[06:48] Sofia: We'll show a short Optimize report now. (shares screen) Here you can see recommendations: reduce batch size for lower latency during bursts, enable prefix caching for session-based chat, and switch to an int8-ish profile for lower per-token cost.
[07:20] Martin: About regional failover: if eu-central hits capacity, can you route to another region? We can't move data outside EU.
[07:27] Jordan: For EU-only data residency you can pin to EU regions and set routing policy to fail closed — we won't route outside EU. If you need cross-region failover you'd need Private deployment or VPC peering with explicit agreements.
[07:45] Priya: Could you walk through a sample request/response while streaming and show how to recompose tokens?
[07:50] Sofia: Yep. (demo code) The stream emits delta tokens roughly every 50-200ms depending on model and response length. Client collects deltas, updates UI incrementally. If you get an error, the last ACKed token index is used to resume. We also show snippets for server-side dedupe with idempotency keys.
[08:30] Olivia: Any notable gotchas around rate limits during POC?
[08:34] Jordan: Default rate limits are conservative for self-serve; for POC we'll bump them. Also watch concurrency: too many parallel short requests can actually hurt throughput compared to batching similar prompts. Optimize will flag hot routes.
[08:58] Martin: Can you do a quick handshake with our DevOps to show how SAML SSO and RBAC is set up?
[09:04] Jordan: Absolutely; we'll include our SSO guide. For RBAC, you can create role templates and restrict console access to read-only, monitor, or admin.
[09:18] Priya: Regarding cost estimates — can you send a simple spreadsheet with tokens per session * projected sessions?
[09:24] Jordan: Yes we'll include a starter cost model. We'll estimate unit tokens, average response length, and burst multipliers.
[09:32] Sofia: Ok demo wrap-up: small checklist for client engineers — (1) integrate streaming client and idempotency keys, (2) instrument partial token displays, (3) implement exponential backoff with jitter, (4) instrument telemetry for Optimize.
[09:50] Martin: This is helpful. A question on QA: how do you help detect quality regressions post-deploy?
[09:55] Jordan: We run prompt set-based evals. You provide a set of prompts and expected outputs; Redwood runs evaluations on each model variant and alerts when quality drops beyond thresholds. That ties into rollouts — canary and automatic rollback policies.
[10:20] Priya: For the POC, can we get a sandbox project and share some prompts?
[10:24] Jordan: Yep, we'll provision a sandbox account and seed it with sample data and console dashboards.
[10:30] Sofia: A quick note on SDKs — they include helpers for stream parsing, token budgeting, and built-in retry examples. Use them to avoid reinventing the wheel.
[10:45] Olivia: About telemetry and privacy: if we send logs to Redwood for Optimize, are they stored?
[10:52] Jordan: By default telemetry is retained short-term, but for enterprise we can configure retention policies and deletion workflows. We'll include that in the security FAQ.
[11:10] Martin: Anything else on retries — do you ever recommend synchronous vs async for heavy generation?
[11:15] Sofia: For longer generations (>5s) we sometimes recommend an async pattern: submit job, poll or webhook callback when ready. Streaming still works for interactive experiences. Async helps decouple user timeout constraints.
[11:34] Jordan: Ok jumping to a simulated error/resume scenario. (demo) We show a stream that stops, the client captures last token, re-issues continuation with idempotency and gets resumed chunk.
[12:00] Priya: Nice. Can you quantify latency percentiles for the model families?
[12:06] Sofia: Example from our perf sheet: p50 ~ 120ms per token for small sequences on dedicated GPUs, p95 ~ 500ms under burst. Hosted numbers vary by region and model; for POC we'll run benchmarks against your typical prompts.
[12:30] Martin: Any immediate blockers for starting the POC?
[12:35] Jordan: Not really — we need an intake form with compliance constraints, and a legal contact for the PO. We can start infra provisioning once those are in.
[12:50] Priya: Would you run a small embedding + retrieval flow as part of POC? We want to test multi-turn context with a vector DB.
[12:57] Sofia: Yes, we can include a retrieval-augmented generation check. We'll demonstrate prefix caching plus embedding calls and show latency effects.
[13:22] Jordan: Wrapping up, we'll send: pricing estimate, SOC2 attestation, streaming retry playbook, and sandbox invite. Any other asks?
[13:35] Martin: Please include a short video of the console tour for our product PM.
[13:38] Jordan: Will do.
[13:42] Olivia: Also include an example of the SDK resume logic for streaming.
[13:45] Sofia: I'll add a gist link in the follow-up.
[13:50] Martin: Great, thanks folks.
[13:54] Jordan: Thanks all — recap of next steps in the follow-up email.

(End of recorded transcript; remaining minutes used for quick one-to-one clarifications and calendar scheduling.)
